1	# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code
2	
3	**seeding**
4	: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").
5	
6	**base build**
7	: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.
8	
9	**old code**
10	: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.
11	
12	Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run compiles into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.
13	
14	## Finding or building a base build
15	
16	- If your brief names a base build, use it.
17	- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
18	  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
19	  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
20	  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
21	- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s. Say so in your report.
22	
23	      git -C /home/user/fortress worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
24	      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
25	      ant compileAll
26	      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
27	      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
28	      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean
29	
30	If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.
31	
32	## Seeding a worktree
33	
34	Every compile rewrites cache files of the tree that it runs in. So compile only into caches that no other agent compiles into. Your brief says where you work. If you need a build of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.
35	
36	Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.
37	
38	    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]
39	
40	- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
41	- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
42	- If the worktree already has a build, the script keeps it. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
43	- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
44	- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
45	- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.
46	
47	## Running the old code
48	
49	If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.
50	
51	`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:
52	
53	    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
54	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
55	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
56	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
57	    $T <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test   # a compiled .test
58	
59	- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
60	- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
61	- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
62	- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).
63	
64	To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:
65	
66	    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
67	        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss
68	
69	The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".
70

1	# The Claude Code session: the Bash tool, long commands, waits and stops
2	
3	**prompt cache**
4	: API's copy of a conversation's context. It lives five minutes for an agent and one hour for the main session. Each request to the API within that time reads the cache and renews it. The first request after a longer wait writes the whole context again: late in a long task, hundreds of thousands of tokens.
5	
6	**interrupt**
7	: Stop of the session's turn, by the stop button. It kills every agent that runs in the background at that moment, of the Agent tool or of a Workflow.
8	
9	**stop of the process**
10	: End of the session's Claude Code process. It kills every agent. It keeps the conversation, the transcripts and the disk: worktrees, uncommitted edits and logs. A command started with `nohup`, as `run_bg` (below) starts it, survives a stop, but not a restart of the machine.
11	
12	**automatic permission check**
13	: Check that approves each tool call in auto mode. It can refuse a call, also a call that the curator approved in chat.
14	
15	## The Bash tool and waits
16	
17	The Bash tool stops a call at 120 s, unless the call passes a longer `timeout`, at most 600 s. It kills the command, or moves it to the background. It also refuses a command that starts with `sleep N` and goes on to another command, such as `sleep 60; tail build.log`. Wait with `wait_for` instead (below).
18	
19	- In an agent, keep every wait under 270 s.
20	- In the main session, keep every wait under an hour. The main session can also watch a run with the `Monitor` tool.
21	
22	## Long commands
23	
24	Two shell functions run a long command:
25	
26	- `run_bg` starts the command detached. It writes the output to the log, then a last line `EXIT=<status>`.
27	- `wait_for` waits for the `EXIT=` line, for 270 s at most. If the line is there, it prints the log's verdict lines and returns 0. If not, it returns 1.
28	
29	If a command can take more than a minute or two, start it with `run_bg`. Then run `wait_for` until it returns 0, each time in a new Bash call. Give that call a `timeout` above 270 s, such as 300000 ms. Grep the log for the lines that you need. Define both functions in each call that uses them:
30	
31	    run_bg () {      # run_bg <logfile> "<command>"
32	        nohup bash -c "( $2 ) > '$1' 2>&1; echo EXIT=\$? >> '$1'" >/dev/null 2>&1 &
33	    }
34	    wait_for () {    # wait_for <logfile> [max seconds, at most 270]; call again until it returns 0
35	        local n=0 max=${2:-270}
36	        case "$max" in ''|*[!0-9]*) max=270 ;; esac ; [ "$max" -gt 270 ] && max=270
37	        while ! grep -q '^EXIT=' "$1" 2>/dev/null ; do
38	            sleep 5 ; n=$((n+5))
39	            [ "$n" -ge "$max" ] && { echo "still running after ${n}s" ; return 1 ; }
40	        done
41	        grep -n '^BUILD \|^Total time:\|^EXIT=' "$1"
42	    }
43	
44	## Stopping processes
45	
46	Stop only the processes that run under your tree's path. To find a process's path, read `readlink /proc/<pid>/cwd`, or the paths in its arguments.
47	
48	Kill by process id, with `kill <pid>`. A pattern, as in `pkill -f`, also matches other agents' copies of the same scripts, and your own call's shell, which it then kills.
49	
50	## After an interrupt or a stop of the process
51	
52	If your work starts again after an interrupt or a stop of the process:
53	
54	1. Read what is on disk first: `git log` and `git status` in your tree, and your logs.
55	2. If a step's log has ended and the tree has not changed since, the step is done. A log has ended if it has its `EXIT=` line, or its verdict or table is complete.
56	3. If a log has no `EXIT=` line yet, its command may still run. Look for its process under your tree's path. If it runs, wait for it with `wait_for`.
57	4. Continue at the first step whose log is missing, cut off or failed.
58	
59	## When the automatic permission check refuses a call
60	
61	- Do not try for the same result with another tool, by another route or in a later turn.
62	- Report the refusal and what was not done because of it. The way through is the curator's: manual approval for the session, or an allow rule for the command (`/permissions`).
63

1	# The interpreter (walk)
2	
3	Walk's code is in `interpreter/`:
4	
5	- `evaluator/`: the tree walker.
6	- `env/`: the environments, which map names to values, and the wrappers that load components and apis.
7	- `rewrite/`: walk's own rewrite of the tree.
8	- `glue/`: the natives.
9	
10	## How walk evaluates a program
11	
12	After the phases (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"), walk rewrites each component in `interpreter/rewrite/`: it gives each reference to a name the lexical depth of its declaration. The evaluator looks up the name by that depth. The compiled path has no such rewrite.
13	
14	At a call of a generic function, walk infers the static arguments from the run-time types of the arguments (`interpreter/evaluator/EvaluatorBase.java`, `inferAndInstantiateGenericFunction`). Each static parameter gets an interval, from a lower to an upper bound, in a `LatticeIntervalMap` (`useful/`). A type in the domain of an arrow type, such as `T` in `T -> ZZ32`, is contravariant. So its bounds go into the dual map, `LatticeIntervalMapDual`: the same table, with the order reversed. `MakeInferenceSpecific` then makes the inferences more specific, in practice only in the dual map.
15	
16	Walk chooses a coercion by the value at run time. The specification and the compiled path choose it statically. This is an accepted limit until the switch-over.
17	
18	## What walk checks
19	
20	Walk does not check static types (`SKILL.md`, "The phases"). No command checks them for a walk program: `fortress typecheck` checks against the compiler's prelude.
21	
22	At load, walk checks the overload sets and some `comprises` clauses. It refuses:
23	
24	- two declarations of one name that its parameter-by-parameter check cannot order. It accepts them if their declared domains order a generic declaration and a plain one, or if `comprises` clauses cover the overlap.
25	- two functional methods that break the Meet Rule for Functional Methods (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`) in a type that provides both.
26	- an overloaded function with one parameter of type `T`, where `T extends Any` is written: `f[\T extends Any\](x: T)`.
27	- an extender that a `comprises` clause of the program's main component does not allow. Walk does not yet check the library's clauses, another component's clauses or an object expression's clauses.
28	
29	So a library edit that adds an overload can stop every program at load. `tests-writing.md` says how a test names a refusal at load.
30	
31	Walk's overload-ambiguity message names its two declarations in an order that varies from run to run. On one core, the order is fixed for a given library, but a library edit can change it. Do not pin or compare this order. The harness reads only that an `XXX` test fails.
32	
33	## Natives
34	
35	The library binds each of walk's natives by a string in its `.fss` files: `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.X")`. The classes are in `interpreter/glue/prim/`. They take the evaluator's boxed values, so the compiled path cannot use them. `import java`, the compiled path's way to bind natives, is wired under walk but unfinished, and no test uses it.
36	
37	To raise a Fortress exception that a Fortress `catch` sees, a native throws a `FortressError` that holds the exception's object. `Int.overflow()` in `Int.java` there makes one, and its callers throw it:
38	
39	    FObject f = (FObject) Driver.getFortressLibrary().getRootValue(WellKnownNames.integerOverflowException);
40	    return new FortressError(f);
41	
42	A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other exception from a native ends the run, a division by zero too.
43	
44	## Running a program
45	
46	    bin/fortress P.fss
47	
48	- If the run stops on an error, it prints the error and the Fortress stack under `Context:`. The hint below them names `-debug interpreter`, which shows nothing more. To see the Java stack too, run `bin/fortress -debug stacktrace P.fss`.
49	- Walk searches for imports in the current directory first (`build-and-caches.md`, "Name resolution").
50	- If `JAVA_FLAGS` is not set, `bin/fortress` uses `-Xmx256m -Xss32m`. Your setup gives a 4 GB heap, and the test harness uses 768 MB. A test can pass at two of these heaps and die at the third. If you claim that a run fails near a memory limit, measure the claim at 256 MB: run with `JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx256m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$PWD/tmp"`.
51	- Your setup sets `FORTRESS_THREADS`, the size of the pool, to 1 (`SKILL.md`, "Parallelism and mutable state"). If it is unset, the pool has half the CPUs.
52	- A small program takes about 8 s with cold caches, and about 4 s with warm caches.
53	- Do not take or record a timing of walk. Do not edit anything to make walk faster.
54	- To check a build, run `bin/fortress explorations/mandelbrot_canonical.fss`, which prints its picture, or `bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss`, which prints nothing and exits 0. Do not use `explorations/claude_demo.fss`: it dies under walk (ledger row 424). `ProjectFortress/hello.fss` runs only on the compiled path.
55	
56	## The model program
57	
58	MicroGPT runs only under walk, by hand, never in the gate. To check the model after a library change, run `explorations/coordinator/tools/mg-run.sh <work-dir> <label> [threads]`. 1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the run time
2	
3	The code of this area is in these directories:
4	
5	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
6	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
7	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
8	
9	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
10	
11	## Which desugarings run on each path
12	
13	Both paths run the same desugaring phases. Inside them, switches in `Shell.java` decide which desugarings run. Walk turns off these desugarings, which the compiled path runs:
14	
15	- coercion;
16	- chained comparisons;
17	- compound and tuple assignment, and subscripts;
18	- case expressions, typecase and type ascription;
19	- the marking of a bodiless declaration as abstract.
20	
21	Walk evaluates those nodes itself, in `interpreter/evaluator/Evaluator.java` (`forChainExpr`, `forAssignment`, `forCaseExpr`, `forTypecase`, `forAsExpr`). It converts by coercion at dispatch, in `OverloadedFunction.bestMatchWithCoercion`. So if you fix one of these desugarers, only the compiled path changes. If walk is wrong there, fix the evaluator.
22	
23	## What the two paths share
24	
25	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
26	
27	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
28	- Number natives: walk's `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`), and the compiled `nativeHelpers/` (`simpleIntArith.java`).
29	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
30	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
31	
32	So a fix of a rule on one path is not a fix on the other. In your report, say which path you fixed, and whether the other path has the same defect.
33	
34	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
35	
36	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
37	
38	- Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay.
39	- The record does not yet say what happens to `CompilerSystem` at the switch-over.
40	
41	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
42	
43	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
44	
45	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
46	- a local function declaration, and an object expression;
47	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
48	
49	It also refuses a function, object or trait declaration with a `where` clause or a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`).
50	
51	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
52	
53	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
54	
55	## What the code generator does
56	
57	`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time", gives the jars, the dispatch methods, the templates and the boxed numbers.
58	
59	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
60	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
61	- The `value` modifier has no effect on the representation.
62	- The curator decided that array storage will be an unboxed `double[]`. This is not built yet. The other questions of the array design wait until after the switch-over. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print both decisions first (about 2 KB):
63	
64	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:Storage is' 'positions:array design'
65	
66	## The run time
67	
68	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Open ledger rows name it, such as rows 408 and 559.
69	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.
70	
71	## Natives
72	
73	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
74	
75	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method.
76	
77	## Traps of the compiled path
78	
79	- Before disambiguation, the compiled path bounds an unbounded type parameter by `Object`, not `Any`. Walk does not. So the compiled path rejects every generic that is instantiated at a tuple type, until the switch-over (ledger row 412).
80	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. The linker looks for a component with the api's own name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
81	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. The team turned it off in 2012 (`c35aac139`). If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
82	
83	## The `fortress` commands
84	
85	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
86	
87	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
88	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
89	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
90	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

1	# The library
2	
3	The library is `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`, without the compiler's own files there:
4	
5	- In `Library/`: the interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary.fss` and `.fsi`, and its other components. The compiler's `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `CompilerSystem` are not part of it. `FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi` are generated from `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast`: edit that file, never these two.
6	- In `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`: `FortressBuiltin`, `NativeArray` and the rest. The compiler's `CompilerBuiltin` is not part of it.
7	- `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType`, the top type, belongs to both libraries. After an edit to it, also take the compiled path's step (`build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library").
8	- `Library/incomplete/` is not on the source path (`default_repository/configuration`), so no program can import what it declares. Nothing that the suites or the model program run imports `Library/GeneratorLibrary.fss` either. Before you cite a declaration as the library's way, check that a running program can reach it.
9	
10	## How loops and reductions call the library
11	
12	The desugarer, which both paths share, turns these forms into calls of the library:
13	
14	- `for x <- g do b end` becomes `g.loop(fn x => b)`, a call of the generator's `loop` method. Each further generator nests one more `loop` call inside.
15	- `while x <- e do b end` becomes `while __whileCond(e, fn x => b) do end`. `if x <- e then ... end` becomes a call of `__cond`.
16	- A comprehension or a big operator, such as `SUM`, becomes a call of `__bigOperator`, whose argument calls `__generate` on each generator. A big operator inside another becomes one call of `__bigOperator2`.
17	
18	These functions work on the library's generators and reductions: `trait Generator` and `trait Reduction` in `FortressLibrary.fsi`, and `RangeInternals.fss` for ranges. `FortressLibrary.fss` also defines `__loop`, but no desugaring calls it. So a failure inside a loop or a reduction is most often in the library's code, and its fix is a library edit.
19	
20	## The curator's decisions on the library
21	
22	- Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only. A range over another integer type is a static error, and walk stops when it builds one. Write a wider counter as a `ZZ32` loop that widens its index.
23	- `ZZ32` and numerals convert into `RR64` implicitly. `ZZ64` converts into `RR64` only explicitly, by `asFloat`.
24	- For arithmetic that wraps on overflow, use the wrapping operators ∔ `DOTPLUS`, ∸ `DOTMINUS` and ⨰ `DOTTIMES`. Parenthesise every such expression fully, because their precedence is stated only among themselves.
25	- `SUM` and `PROD` are generic over `AdditiveGroup` and `MultiplicativeRing`. If nothing at the call fixes the element type, write it: `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Under walk, a call without it fails at its first element (ledger row 424).
26	- An array's `fill` takes a value, and its `tabulate` a function of the index: `array[\ZZ32\](4).fill(0)`, `array[\ZZ32\](4).tabulate(fn (i:ZZ32):ZZ32 => 10 i)`. The factories that take a function are `tabulatedArray1` to `tabulatedArray3` and `tabulatedVector`.
27	
28	## Designing a change
29	
30	- Put each extension into this library, outside the compiler's files. This includes an extension that only the model program needs.
31	- Fix a gap in the library, not by a workaround in the program that meets it. The library's practice gives the design, not the specification's text alone.
32	- If a rule of the language or the checker refuses the way that you want, find how the library writes that kind of thing. Do the same.
33	- If the library's practice and the specification's text disagree, do as `specification.md`, "When the text and an implementation disagree", says.
34	- When you add a method, make it dotted or functional as its family in the library does. If the family shows no practice, follow the team's proposal (`Library/incomplete/Collection.fss`): an updater, a getter or a setter, indexing included, is dotted, and every other method is functional.
35	- A new functional method reserves its name in every program that imports the library. The phase that binds names then refuses each program that names a variable or a parameter after it: "Variable even is already declared."
36	- A dotted method shadows a top-level function of the same name (`overloading.tex`, "Principles of Overloading").
37	
38	## Editing
39	
40	A comment after a declaration that ends in an expression or a type becomes part of that declaration's source span. It also becomes part of the unambiguous name made from the span. So a comment-only edit changes the syntax tree. Before you compare parse trees or diagnostics across such an edit, map their positions back to the lines before the edit. Three removed scripts did this: `parse-compare.sh`, `ast-compare.py` and `remap-lines.py`. Print one with `git show ab067d9b6^:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-library-comments/<name>`.
41

34	
35	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
36	
37	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`.
38	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
39	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
40	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
41	  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

1	# Exploring: a question that the record does not settle
2	
3	The record keeps what earlier workers found, and they met many of the same questions. Workers have called a thing absent or new when the record already held it.
4	
5	## The choices that are yours
6	
7	The curator settles every conflict and every question about a decision of the curator. Any other choice is yours only if it meets all four of these conditions:
8	
9	- It changes only one area.
10	- It changes no line of the model program.
11	- It changes no decision of the curator.
12	- It can be undone.

14	## The procedure
15	
16	1. Search the record with the queries in `records.md`. If two of the team's sources disagree, also load `revival-changes.md`.
17	2. If the record or `revival-changes.md` settles the question, go back to building. Cite what settles it.
18	3. If you have evidence against a decision of the curator, read its POSITIONS entry and the notes that it names. If the decision used your evidence, go back to building.
19	4. Search the original tree.
20	5. Before you write that something does not exist, search the record for it, INDEX included (`index:WORDS`).
21	6. Record what you found as `tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", says. For an open question, follow its item 3.
22	7. If your brief does not let you edit the ledger, put the ledger row in your report:
23	   1. Write the row in a file, in the form that `records.md` gives for a new row.
24	   2. Run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py check --rows FILE`. It counts the `?` in the number cell as a broken rule. Correct the row until the check names no other rule.
25	   3. Copy the row into your report.
26	8. If the question touches a passage of the specification, also record what `specification.md` asks for.
27	9. If the choice is yours, make it. Report it as a decision.
28	10. If the choice is the curator's, report it as a decision not taken. Give these:
29	    - the question;
30	    - each source, and its date (`specification.md`, "Weighing the sources", says what else to note);
31	    - each possible solution, and what it changes;
32	    - which solution keeps the current behaviour.
33	11. If you cannot get some evidence in your task, say in your report what is missing and how to get it.

1	# The specification
2	
3	Three folders hold the team's specification:
4	
5	- `Specification/` is the team's text, as the revival revises it. It says what the language means, except where a decision of the curator says otherwise.
6	- `Specification-1.0-frozen/` is the unrevised copy. Cite it as "the Working Draft of February 2011". Only `fortress.1.0.pdf` in it is the 1.0 release. Leave this copy unchanged.
7	- `Documentation/Specification/` is the team's later restart, which they did not finish. If its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, cite it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word.
8	
9	Appendix I, `Specification/appendices/changes.tex`, records the changes to the text. Its revival section has one entry for each change that the revival made.
10	
11	A draft build prints the team's `\note{}` boxes, and a release build hides them. Many say that a feature was not built, for example "Reduction variables are not yet supported." Before you record a missing feature as a gap, grep the notes of its chapter: `grep -n '\\note{' Specification/<file>.tex`.
12	
13	The api listings of the library part are generated from the library's `.fsi` files when the specification is built (`Specification/library/apis/`, not in the tree). A listing shows the library itself, so it cannot justify a change of the library. Cite the `.fsi` file.
14	
15	## Weighing the sources
16	
17	The type group is the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, from 2010 to 2012. Where their late positions disagree with the specification's earlier text, the curator gives the late positions more weight. These positions are:
18	
19	- the exclusion rule;
20	- compiled code specialised to each instantiation of a generic, which they kept;
21	- the compiled number tower, which they flattened in 2011;
22	- the 2012 write-up on the Return Type Rule (`Papers/Types/journal/`);
23	- the POPL 2019 paper on symmetric multiple dispatch (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md`).
24	
25	When your report describes the team's sources on a question (`exploring.md`), say which of them is one of these positions.
26	
27	If a conflict or a decision not taken needs the designers' reason for a rule, print the row of its design area. WORD is a word of the area, such as `coercion`, `juxtaposition`, `dispatch` or `Arrays`. A word can match several rows, each about 1 to 2 KB.
28	
29	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:design-intent-sources.md#The map, by design area@WORD'
30	
31	Then open the sources that the row names. Among them are the `\note{}` boxes and the team's written rationale in the Internal Document appendix: `Specification/appendices/FAQ.tex` and `future.tex`.
32	
33	## Changing the text: the revision form
34	
35	Every change of the text has the four parts below, so that no disagreement between the text and an implementation stays hidden.
36	
37	1. At each changed passage, a callout that prints in every build, unlike a `\note`:
38	
39	       \revision{<label>}{<what changed, in a sentence or two>}
40	
41	   `<label>` is the `\seclabel` of the change's Appendix I entry.
42	
43	2. An entry in the revival section of Appendix I: a `\subsection` with a `\seclabel`. The entry gives:
44	   - the affected sections, the change, its rationale and its effect;
45	   - the original text, quoted with its path and line in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`;
46	   - what a reversal to the alternative not taken would need;
47	   - the decision of the curator that it follows (its POSITIONS entry), or the reason that your brief gives.
48	
49	   For the form, print one entry, about 2 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:Specification/appendices/changes.tex#choice of a coercion'`.
50	
51	3. The front matter's one paragraph on the revision, in `Specification/fortress/preamble.tex`. If your change makes it false, correct it.
52	
53	4. The full reasoning, in a decision record under `explorations/`: each changed passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. For the form, print one passage of an earlier record, about 4 KB: `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md#3.3'`.
54	
55	If the revision refuses an example, keep the example in the text, marked "Not allowed", as the specification itself does. If your change contradicts a calculus of Appendix A, keep the calculus's rules and soundness claims. Add a callout to it that says what it predates.
56	
57	## When the text and an implementation disagree
58	
59	- If a decision of the curator says which side is correct, change the other side to agree.
60	- If no decision says so, the disagreement is a conflict. Switch to exploring (`exploring.md`).
61	- If the passage has an Appendix I entry, add the conflict's ledger row to the departures that its effect lists. Then the text claims no more than holds.
62	
63	## Citing it
64	
65	- If your change renames or removes a section that a test names, update that citation in the same commit.
66	- Inside the text, cite a section with `\secref{label}`.

11	## Generated sources
12	
13	These generated sources are committed:
14	
15	- `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` generates `nodes/`, `scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, and `Library/FortressAst.fss` and `.fsi`.
16	- The parser grammars generate the parsers.

1	# What the revival changed in the team's Fortress
2	
3	The team left three forms of Fortress, which disagree in places:
4	
5	- the specification;
6	- walk, with the interpreter's library;
7	- the compiled path, with the compiler's library.
8	
9	This part lists each change of the revival made for one of two reasons: two of the team's sources contradict each other, or a program failed. Its headings are the points of `SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language", that the changes qualify.
10	
11	Each resolution is a decision of the curator. Where it changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. `specification.md`, "Weighing the sources", describes the type group, whose later texts most resolutions follow.
12	
13	If a source of the team's, an old note or your training disagrees with this skill, find the point below. If it is there, follow the skill: it describes the tree. If it is not, do as `SKILL.md`, "When to explore", says.
14	
15	A note written before the revival, and your training, can be right about the team's walk and out of date here. Three examples: the number types form a tower, fixed-width arithmetic wraps, and walk converts no argument.
16	
17	## Dispatch is on every argument, at run time
18	
19	**Overloads that differ in static parameters**
20	
21	- Original: the Working Draft forbids two declarations of one name whose static parameters differ, beside the team's note "This restriction will be relaxed." Neither implementation enforced it, and the checker implements the type group's 2011 paper (`Papers/Types/`), which allows them.
22	- Resolution: such overloads are allowed, and the specification states the paper's model.
23	- Reason: the implementations and the library already allow such overloads. Enforcing the sentence would refuse about 180 pairs of declarations in the library's apis.
24	
25	**The return-type rule**
26	
27	- Original: the type group's 2011 paper asks for the rule on every instance of a generic declaration. The checker tested one instance, so a pair that broke the rule compiled, and its run failed the JVM's verification.
28	- Resolution: the checker tests every instance.
29	- Reason: the paper's rule. Such a program now fails at compile time, not at run time.
30	
31	**Walk's choice between a generic and a plain declaration**
32	
33	- Original: the Working Draft chooses the most specific declaration by the declared parameter types. Walk chose by the order in which the declarations were written.
34	- Resolution: walk chooses by the declared types.
35	- Reason: the specification's rule. A program's answer no longer depends on the order of its declarations.
36	
37	**`fill` and `tabulate`**
38	
39	- Original: the interpreter's library declared two array methods named `fill`: one takes a value, one a function of the index. For an element type of `Any` or of a function type, both apply and neither is more specific. The checker refused the pair, and walk called a function meant as the value.
40	- Resolution: the function form is `tabulate` (`library.md`).
41	- Reason: a second name ends the ambiguity. Scala's `Array.fill` and `Array.tabulate` have the same two meanings.
42	
43	## Traits and objects, no classes
44	
45	**The exclusion rule**
46	
47	- Original: the type group's papers and the checker have the exclusion rule. The Working Draft does not state it, and some of its examples break it.
48	- Resolution: the specification states the rule. It keeps the examples that break it, marked "Not allowed".
49	- Reason: without it, the checker's return-type rule lets through programs that die with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`. The later Types chapter states the rule too.
50	
51	**What a `comprises` clause says**
52	
53	- Original: four passages of the Working Draft read the clause as a statement about types, and so are false for some programs that it allows. The type group's later Types chapter reads the clause as a statement about values.
54	- Resolution: every value of the closed trait is a value of a listed type. A generic trait may extend the closed trait without being listed, if each type that extends it is below a listed type.
55	- Reason: read by values, the passages hold for those programs.
56	
57	## Static parameters
58	
59	**The bound of a type parameter that has none written**
60	
61	- Original: the Working Draft bounds it by `Object`. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuples, such as arrays indexed by pairs, and `Object` holds no tuple.
62	- Resolution: the bound is `Any`. The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over (`compiler.md`, "Traps of the compiled path").
63	- Reason: the library works only with `Any`.
64	
65	**A type parameter that a call does not fix**
66	
67	- Original: the implementations gave it the empty type `Bottom`, or left it unsolved, and some such compiled calls failed the JVM's verification. The type group's POPL 2019 paper gives such a parameter its bound.
68	- Resolution: it takes its bound. Under walk, a parameter whose bound names the parameter itself, such as `SUM`'s, still gets `Bottom` (ledger row 424).
69	- Reason: the paper is the type group's latest word on the rule.
70	
71	**Sizes on the compiled path**
72	
73	- Original: the Working Draft has the size parameters `nat` and `int`. The checker crashed on sized declarations, and a sized program did not compile or load. The team's code generator had reserved a slot for a size's run-time descriptor.
74	- Resolution: the checker checks sizes, and the slot holds the size's descriptor (`SKILL.md`, "The compiled run time").
75	- Reason: it completes the team's design, which carries a size as it carries a type argument.
76	
77	## Numbers are siblings, not a tower
78	
79	**Tower or siblings**
80	
81	- Original: the interpreter's library nested the number types: `ZZ32` extended `ZZ64`, which extended `ZZ`. The compiler's library had them as siblings. The tower breaks the exclusion rule: `ZZ32` was an `Integral[\ZZ32\]` and, through `ZZ64`, an `Integral[\ZZ64\]`.
82	- Resolution: the library makes them siblings, as the compiler's library does.
83	- Reason: the exclusion rule stays (above), so the tower cannot.
84	
85	**Conversion under walk**
86	
87	- Original: the Working Draft converts a call's arguments by coercion when that makes the call apply, and the checker does so. Walk converted nothing: its dispatch code held the team's note "TODO add checks for COERCE".
88	- Resolution: walk converts by coercion at a call, a typed binding and an assignment. `interpreter.md` says how it chooses the coercion.
89	- Reason: the specification's rule, which the siblings need for every mix of widths.
90	
91	**Mixed number types in a generic call**
92	
93	- Original: neither implementation inferred a static argument through a conversion, and the Working Draft's chapter on inference is a heading and two notes. The tower needed no conversion there: a `ZZ32` was a `ZZ64`.
94	- Resolution: if the arguments of one type parameter mix number types, it takes the narrowest type into which all of them convert. For a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` that is `ZZ64`, and for a `ZZ32` and an `NN32` too.
95	- Reason: among siblings, only a conversion joins two widths.
96	
97	**Overflow**
98	
99	- Original: the Working Draft and the compiled path raise `IntegerOverflow` when a fixed-width result does not fit. Walk wrapped the result.
100	- Resolution: walk raises `IntegerOverflow` too. Code that means to wrap uses the specification's wrapping operators (`library.md`).
101	- Reason: the specification and the compiled path already agreed.
102	
103	**Ranges**
104	
105	- Original: the interpreter's ranges took any integer type. The compiler's library had ranges over `ZZ32` only.
106	- Resolution: ranges are over `ZZ32` only (`library.md`).
107	- Reason: a range counts the indices of an array, and a JVM array index is a 32-bit `int`.
108	
109	**`SUM` and `PROD`**
110	
111	- Original: `SUM` and `PROD` reduced over `Number`, under the team's comment "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically". Every sum had the type `Number`, and an empty sum of `RR64` values was the integer 0.
112	- Resolution: each is one generic declaration over the element type's own algebra, which gives its zero or one at that type (`library.md`).
113	- Reason: `Number`'s operators for any number went with the tower, so each reduction uses the element type's own operator.
114

- Tracks and shards: `build.xml:930-998, :1171-1213`; CompilerJUTest/LibraryJUTest sweep: `explorations/coordinator/test-discipline.md` § 5.
- Times and counts: the gate summary (testFast 11 min 11 s, 1,815; testSystem 3 min 46 s, 516); brief-machine:16-17 (635 s, 243 s); exploration § 4 gate row (541 s, 165 s).
- Never both at once: the script `:1799`; map test-coverage D.1 (shared test-caches); `build.xml:964, :1205` (each deletes test.caches).
- Results path: `build.xml:128`; `explorations/repo-internals.md:225-226`.
- BUILD SUCCESSFUL equivalence: the script `:1800` (gate step 5).
- FORTRESS_THREADS pinned, 768 MB: FACTS "The gate's thread count is pinned in the build file"; `build.xml:131`. Temporary files in `ProjectFortress/test-tmp`: the `fastTrack` and `systemShard` macros (`-Djava.io.tmpdir=${PF}/test-tmp`).
- Shards by sorted index, compare sum; count down means missing .test: FACTS "`testSystem`'s four shards are one suite split by sorted index"; the script `:1800`.
- harness-one.sh: its header and body, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh`; times: exploration § 2 (15-16 s for three), § 6 (25 s on old code). Passing X.test beside X.fss: inferred from the script copying every argument and `FileTests.java:841-860` reading `Name.test` beside `Name.fss`.
- Direct run for diagnostics: `explorations/repo-internals.md:231-233`; heaps: FACTS "Three heaps run the interpreter".
- junit.sh: its header and body, `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/merged-tests/junit.sh:1-29`; one JVM together: the manual "Rules weighed", item 6. The cold read's finding 2.1: `climb-batch-N` is the folder of climb batch N (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-N.md`), and `ls explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-*/merged-tests/junit.sh` finds one copy; the label is printed in the output's lines (`:19`, `:24`) and the script writes to standard output only; it removes the named components' cache entries (`:15-16`, `:29`); it sources env.sh (`:10`) and runs `java $JAVA_FLAGS` (`:20`, `:25`). The same list in one JVM by hand: `Shell junit` passes its arguments to `FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles` (`Shell.java:1086`) and returns 0 whatever the verdict (`:1088`).
- `fortress junit` by hand, testOnly, switches: map test-coverage D.2; `build.xml:777-812`; `FileTests.java:909, :1220, :1244, :1256`.
- One whole-suite run per code state, no partial stage runs: the script `:1035-1039` ("a code state is a commit of the branch, and only a commit that changes code starts a new one"); who reads the result is no longer said. The rule names the checker's and walk's source; the code generator is not named (the cold read, finding 1.11, put to the curator), so the part gives it its own tests, the atomic runs where `compiler.md` asks for them, and the gate. The gate's run on a tree that holds other changes is another code state: the prefix's definition of a code state. Whether an agent runs the gate is its brief's (the role-neutral entry under SKILL.md).
- One track by hand: the `fastTrack` macro `build.xml:930-958` (properties, env, memory); `harness-one.sh` (the same pattern for SystemJUTest, global.map seed); `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-overloading-checker/REPORT.md:438` (tracks run as one JVM each with a private cache tree through `junit.textui.TestRunner`); `CompilerJUTest.java:22-24` (main runs TestRunner); compiler track 428 s: map test-coverage D.1. The command itself is composed from these, not copied from one script. `testCompiler`/`testLibrary`/`testOtherCompiler` depend on `cleanCache, compile`: `build.xml:818, :844, :869, :588`.
- Complete log stands: the manual "Shared prefix" (resumed worker paragraph).
- Outside the gate: FACTS "`ant testSpecData` runs 130 of the specification's 133 extracted examples under walk ..." and POSITIONS "The specification's examples join the gate at zero red."; `build.xml:988`, `:1114`, `:1139` (`testNotPassing` and `testSpecData` depend on `compileAll`); `explorations/coordinator/map/test-coverage.md:228`; FACTS "The gate: two corpora, hand-ported ..." (the orphaned folders); `explorations/repo-internals.md:62-68`.
- Track and code state defined first; the suites' facts before their rules; warnings before their commands: the structure comment.
- Why each track has its own caches folder, and the step "after you edit Java, Scala or a grammar, run `ant compileAll` before a suite": the curator's comments of 2026-10-08 on the review page. Checked: the `fastTrack` macro's comment, `build.xml:921-929` (tracks cannot corrupt each other).
- What the suites do not check: `explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md`, item A12, at the curator's approval of 2026-10-08 on the review page; `map/test-coverage.md` C.1 and C.3 (dated 2026-09-16). Checked: nothing outside `bin/BytecodeOptimize` calls `ByteCodeOptimizer` (`git grep`), and `default_repository/configuration:51` turns its tests off; no `grammar` declaration in a test folder. The linker's aliasing, `unparse` and the cache round trip are taken from the map, not re-checked.
- The rewrite of 2026-10-08, a trial of the register (settled by the coordinator): `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`; the new facts from `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/testing-practices.md`, practices 2 and 5, each checked in the code. Shard i of n: `FileTests.java:907-923`. Results in `fast-<track>/` and `system-<i>/`: `build.xml:934, :1175`. The 32 MB stack: `build.xml:39, :949, :1190`. The verbose switch per class: `SystemJUTest.java:34`, `CompilerJUTest.java:38`. The reset switch: `CompilerJUTest.java:32`, `LibraryJUTest.java:32`, `build.xml:944`. Exit 0 whatever the verdict: each class's `main` calls `junit.textui.TestRunner.run` (`SystemJUTest.java:26`, `CompilerJUTest.java:25`). The scratch directory deleted twice, the relative path, the frames removed: `harness-one.sh` lines 9, 14, 16, 18. Frames removed and lines cut at 240: `junit.sh:20, :25`.
- The pass of 2026-10-08 by the cold read `explorations/reviews/skills-cold-read-testing-parts.md` and the curator's comments of 2026-10-08 ("a parser grammar (`parser/*.rats`)"; "DSL grammar"). `junit.sh`'s deletion stated where the script is first offered, bounded to runs that import a DSL grammar (W1; `junit.sh:10`, `env.sh:10`). The code state run on the commit that holds the last edit, "the tests that it reaches" for "the suite", "your own tests" for "its own tests", a library edit named among the other changes (W5, W6, W8): the script `:1035-1039`. One suite at a time in a tree: `build.xml:964, :1205` (S16). `-D` switches on the `java` line: the `fastTrack` and `systemShard` macros pass only their own `sysproperty`s (S13). The harness needs `ProjectFortress/build/`: `harness-one.sh:12` (S1). The track command for another class (S12).
- The build of `4e0f34421` and `840368f92` (`build-efficiency.md` section 7, as the coordinator's brief gives it): the suites build first and pin four threads and `JAVA_FLAGS` (`build.xml:1167-1168`, `:1182`, `:1412`, `:1425`); the step to build before a suite, and the warnings on `testSpecData` and on `junit.sh` sourcing env.sh, dropped; `harness-one.sh`'s kept cache, `COLD_CACHE=1`, four threads and absolute path (`harness-one.sh:7-36`); `junit.sh`'s own settings (`junit.sh:10-20`); the per-corpus targets in place of the hand-made track command (`build.xml:1065-1107`; `build-efficiency.md` 3.10); the compiler track's time from section 6.2 (510 to 515 s).
- The cold read of 2026-10-08, `skills-cold-read-architecture.md`: a shared phase or the parser runs both suites (finding 1, settled by the coordinator for the shared phases; the parser added by the writer, as phase 1 reaches both paths); the run once per code state with no commit needed, and "code state" redefined by an edit of code (finding 4, settled by the coordinator); the test target's build emptying the caches (finding 5); `junit.sh` removes entries before and after the whole list and builds nothing (finding 7 and assumption 6; `junit.sh`, its two `clean` calls around the list and its `java` lines); the `java` line of `harness-one.sh` as the model for `-D` switches (row 12); the ant targets' verdict and exit code (row 13); the atomic runs pointed to `gate.md`; "either library" (row 10).
- After a checker edit, `ant testQuick` in place of "the compiler and library tracks" (settled by the coordinator, 2026-10-08, from the writer's decision not taken): it runs the three compiled tracks at once (`build.xml:1107`), in about the wall time of the longest.

content.content:
<!-- testOnly once left out compileAll, because compileAll flushed the
       cache, which ruled out pinning down cache corruption bugs.
       compileAll now keeps the caches unless the implementation changes
       ("The caches and the implementation"), so testOnly builds first and
       never runs stale classes. -->
  <target name="testOnly" depends="compileAll"
          description="Run specific tests (use -DtestPattern=...).">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <junit printsummary="off"
           haltonerror="off"
           haltonfailure="off"
           showoutput="yes"
           fork="true"
           maxmemory="${junitMem}"
           errorProperty="tests.failed"
           failureProperty="tests.failed">
      <classpath refid="compile.classpath"/>
      <jvmarg value="-Djava.io.tmpdir=${PF}/test-tmp" />
      <jvmarg value="${bigStack}" />
      <formatter type="plain" usefile="false"/>
      <syspropertyset>
        <propertyref prefix="plt." />
      </syspropertyset>
      <batchtest fork="true" todir="${test.results}">
        <fileset dir="${build}">
          <and>
            <filename name="**/*${testPattern}*/**" />
            <or>
              <filename name="**/*JUTest.class" />
              <filename name="**/*JUTestAll.class" />
              <filename name="**/*JxTest.class" />
            </or>
          </and>
          <exclude name="**/*$*.class"/>
        </fileset>
      </batchtest>
    </junit>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <target name="test" depends="compileAll, testFast, testLibrary"
          description="Clean, compile everything, and run all unit and system tests.">
  </target>

  <!-- The per-corpus targets run their corpus as testFast's tracks do
       (fastTrack, below: private caches, the same JVM settings), after an
       incremental build. Each starts its own tracks' caches empty and leaves
       the other tracks' and default_repository/caches alone. -->
  <target name ="testCompiler" depends="compileAll"
          description="Test the native code generator: testFast's compiler and othercompiler tracks">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}/fast-compiler"/>
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}/fast-othercompiler"/>
    <parallel threadcount="2">
      <fastTrack id="compiler">
        <include name="**/CompilerJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="othercompiler">
        <include name="**/OtherCompilerJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
    </parallel>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <target name ="testOtherCompiler" depends="compileAll"
          description="Test the native code generator on other_compiler_tests: testFast's othercompiler track">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}/fast-othercompiler"/>
    <fastTrack id="othercompiler">
      <include name="**/OtherCompilerJUTest.class"/>
    </fastTrack>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <target name ="testLibrary" depends="compileAll"
          description="Test the compiler libraries: testFast's library track">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}/fast-library"/>
    <fastTrack id="library">
      <include name="**/LibraryJUTest.class"/>
    </fastTrack>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <target name ="testQuick" depends="compileAll"
          description="Test the native code generator: testFast's compiler, othercompiler and library tracks">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}/fast-compiler"/>
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}/fast-othercompiler"/>
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}/fast-library"/>
    <parallel threadcount="3">
      <fastTrack id="compiler">
        <include name="**/CompilerJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="othercompiler">
        <include name="**/OtherCompilerJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="library">
        <include name="**/LibraryJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
    </parallel>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <!-- One track of the parallel testFast run: a forked JUnit JVM whose
       cache tree is redirected to a private directory under ${test.caches}
       (sysproperty for in-JVM code, environment variable for the fortress
       processes the tests fork), so tracks cannot corrupt each other or
       the tracked default_repository/caches. Per-suite resets are
       disabled: each track starts cold in a fresh directory.
       FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is pinned here, as in systemShard below. Fortress
       runs tuple elements, arguments and for iterations in parallel by
       default, so the tests run in parallel too: a test that fails or
       varies under parallelism is then found, not hidden by one thread.
       The pin makes the thread count a property of this target, the same
       on any machine, and not of the shell that called ant (unpinned, the
       default is half the CPUs).
       JAVA_FLAGS is pinned for the same reason: a compiled test's run step
       is a bin/fortress run process, which takes its heap and stack from
       JAVA_FLAGS, else from bin/run's default with the JVM's 1 MB thread
       stacks.  Above one thread the program runs on the pool's worker
       threads, and library_tests/TimingRungT, whose recursion is 1,000
       calls deep with its operands forked, overflowed such a stack in 8 of
       12 runs at four threads, and in none of 12 with this value, the
       heap and stack that explorations/experiment/env.sh exports. -->
  <macrodef name="fastTrack">
    <attribute name="id"/>
    <element name="tests" implicit="yes"/>
    <sequential>
      <mkdir dir="${test.results}/fast-@{id}"/>
      <junit printsummary="on"
             haltonerror="off"
             haltonfailure="off"
             showoutput="yes"
             fork="true"
             maxmemory="${junitMem}"
             errorProperty="tests.failed"
             failureProperty="tests.failed">
        <classpath refid="compile.classpath"/>
        <sysproperty key="fortress.junit.reset" value="false"/>
        <sysproperty key="fortress.caches" value="${test.caches}/fast-@{id}"/>
        <env key="FORTRESS_CACHES" value="${test.caches}/fast-@{id}"/>
        <env key="FORTRESS_THREADS" value="4"/>
        <env key="JAVA_FLAGS"
             value="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=${basedir}/${PF}/test-tmp"/>
        <jvmarg value="-Djava.io.tmpdir=${PF}/test-tmp" />
        <jvmarg value="${bigStack}" />
        <formatter type="plain" usefile="true"/>
        <batchtest fork="true" todir="${test.results}/fast-@{id}">
          <fileset dir="${build}">
            <tests/>
          </fileset>
        </batchtest>
      </junit>
    </sequential>
  </macrodef>

  <target name="testFast" depends="compileAll"
          description="Run all unit and system tests expected to pass.">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}"/>
    <!-- The three big suites each dominate a track; everything else shares
         the fourth. Wall clock is the slowest single suite, not the sum. -->
    <parallel threadcount="4">
      <fastTrack id="compiler">
        <include name="**/CompilerJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="library">
        <include name="**/LibraryJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="othercompiler">
        <include name="**/OtherCompilerJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
      <fastTrack id="misc">
        <include name="**/*JUTest.class"/>
        <include name="**/*JUTests.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/CompilerJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/LibraryJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/OtherCompilerJUTest.class"/>

        <!-- Do not run the interpreter tests here. Only run the interpreter
             tests during nightly and CruiseControl testing. -->
        <exclude name="**/TopLevelEnvGenJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/NightlyCompilerJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/SpecDataJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/SystemJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/*$*.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/SyntaxAbstractionJUTestAll.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/ObjectExpressionVisitorJUTest.class"/>
        <exclude name="**/tools/AstJUTest.class"/>
      </fastTrack>
    </parallel>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <target name="testUntil"
          depends="compileAll"
          description="Run all unit and system tests expected to pass, halting on any errors or failures.">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>

<target name="testNotPassing" depends="compileAll"
          description="Run system tests that aren't passing yet.">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <junit printsummary="on"
           haltonerror="off"
           haltonfailure="off"
           showoutput="yes"
           fork="true"
           maxmemory="${junitMem}"
           errorProperty="tests.failed"
           failureProperty="tests.failed">
      <classpath refid="compile.classpath"/>
      <jvmarg value="-Djava.io.tmpdir=${PF}/test-tmp" />
      <formatter type="brief" usefile="true"/>
      <batchtest fork="true" todir="${test.results}">
        <fileset dir="${build}">
          <include name="**/*NotPassingYet.class"/>
        </fileset>
      </batchtest>
    </junit>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to fail are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <target name="testSpecData" depends="compileAll"
          description="Run SpecDataJUTests.">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <junit printsummary="on"
           haltonerror="off"
           haltonfailure="off"
           showoutput="yes"
           fork="true"
           maxmemory="${junitMem}"
           errorProperty="tests.failed"
           failureProperty="tests.failed">
      <classpath refid="compile.classpath"/>
      <jvmarg value="-Djava.io.tmpdir=${PF}/test-tmp" />
      <formatter type="plain" usefile="true"/>
      <batchtest fork="true" todir="${test.results}">
        <fileset dir="${build}">
          <include name="**/SpecDataJUTest.class"/>
        </fileset>
      </batchtest>
    </junit>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

  <!-- testSystem once left out compileAll, because compileAll cleaned the
       cache; compileAll now keeps the caches unless the implementation
       changes, so testSystem builds first, as testFast does. -->

  <!-- One shard of the parallel testSystem run. The shard spec "i/n" makes
       FileTests.interpreterSuite keep every n-th test (by sorted index,
       offset i). Caches are redirected as in fastTrack; FORTRESS_THREADS=4
       is pinned for the reason given there: the tests run in parallel, as
       Fortress does, on any machine. -->
  <macrodef name="systemShard">
    <attribute name="shard"/>
    <attribute name="id"/>
    <sequential>
      <mkdir dir="${test.results}/system-@{id}"/>
      <junit printsummary="on"
             haltonerror="off"
             haltonfailure="off"
             showoutput="yes"
             fork="true"
             maxmemory="${junitMem}"
             errorProperty="tests.failed"
             failureProperty="tests.failed">
        <classpath refid="compile.classpath"/>
        <sysproperty key="fortress.suite.shard" value="@{shard}"/>
        <sysproperty key="fortress.caches" value="${test.caches}/system-@{id}"/>
        <env key="FORTRESS_CACHES" value="${test.caches}/system-@{id}"/>
        <env key="FORTRESS_THREADS" value="4"/>
        <jvmarg value="-Djava.io.tmpdir=${PF}/test-tmp" />
        <jvmarg value="${bigStack}" />
        <formatter type="plain" usefile="true"/>
        <batchtest fork="true" todir="${test.results}/system-@{id}">
          <fileset dir="${build}">
            <include name="**/SystemJUTest.class"/>
          </fileset>
        </batchtest>
      </junit>
    </sequential>
  </macrodef>

  <target name="testSystem" depends="compileAll"
          description="Run SystemJUTests.">
    <mkdir dir="${test.results}"/>
    <mkdir dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <delete quiet="true" dir="${test.caches}"/>
    <parallel threadcount="4">
      <systemShard id="0" shard="0/4"/>
      <systemShard id="1" shard="1/4"/>
      <systemShard id="2" shard="2/4"/>
      <systemShard id="3" shard="3/4"/>
    </parallel>
    <delete dir="${PF}/test-tmp" />
    <fail message="Tests expected to pass are failing!" if="tests.failed"/>
  </target>

185:Before: `testCompiler`, `testOtherCompiler`, `testLibrary` and `testQuick` each had `depends="cleanCache, compile"` and one `<junit>` batch over their classes, in `default_repository/caches`, with no thread pin, and the classes' own reset of those caches (`fortress.junit.reset` unset, so `Shell.resetRepository`).
187:After: `depends="compileAll"`, and each runs its corpus as testFast's tracks: `fastTrack id="compiler"` and `"othercompiler"` (in parallel) for `testCompiler`, `"othercompiler"` for `testOtherCompiler`, `"library"` for `testLibrary`, all three in parallel for `testQuick`. Each deletes only its own tracks' folders under `ProjectFortress/test-caches` first.
189:- What it changes: they build first, and they no longer delete or reset `default_repository/caches`. `ant testLibrary` is exactly testFast's library track, with the gate's JVM settings, so the hand-made track recipe of the skill is no longer needed. Their results are in `TEST-RESULTS/fast-<track>/`, not in `TEST-RESULTS/`.
190:- Why it is safe: the tracks run the same macro as the gate's `testFast`.
192:### 3.11 `fastTrack` and `testFast` (lines 921-966)
205:Before: the comment at 1164-1165 ("testSystem used to have compileAll as a target, but now does not as this cleans the cache."), the comment at 1169 ("FORTRESS_THREADS=1 stops four interpreter runtimes from oversubscribing the CPUs"), the pin at 1188, and `<target name="testSystem"` with no dependency. After: the first comment says testSystem builds first, as testFast does; the second gives the pin of 4 the reason given in `fastTrack`; the pin is `value="4"`; `testSystem` has `depends="compileAll"`.
207:- What 3.11 and 3.12 change: both suites build first, incrementally, so a Java edit is compiled before the suite runs (section 5). The tests run at four threads. Each suite still deletes `ProjectFortress/test-caches` at its start, so the tracks and shards start empty, as before (item 5, section 8).
212:One line, `/default_repository/caches/implementation.stamp`, beside the line for `global.map`. The file lists each cache folder rather than the caches folder, so without the line every tree would show the stamp as untracked, and `seed-worktree.sh`, which refuses a base with changes under `default_repository`, would refuse every built base.
264:- `FORTRESS_THREADS` was 1, from env.sh. It is 4 now, the pin of `fastTrack`, whose tracks the script's `ONE_JVM=1` mode imitates (its header). Question 2 too.
399:`TimingRungT.fss:39` is `countDown(n: ZZ32): ZZ32 = if n <= zero() then zero() else one() + countDown(n - one()) end`, called with 1,000. The code under `ProjectFortress`, `Library` and `bin` is the same as at `b5cde136e`, on which `suites-at-four-threads.md` passed this test. Its run step, 12 times each, with the track's caches:
414:- `ant testFast`, load 2.02 at the start: its build printed `yes`, `yes` and `kept`, then `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, `Total time: 8 minutes 42 seconds`. 1,815 tests: compiler 1,043 (515 s), library 86 (344 s), othercompiler 263 (354 s), misc 423 over 45 classes. All 48 rows equal the gate's.
430:  then `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, `Total time: 8 minutes 57 seconds`. 1,815 tests: compiler 1,043 (510 s), library 86 (344 s), othercompiler 263 (351 s), misc 423. All 48 rows equal the gate's.
437:`ant testLibrary` on `767ba4a3b`, load 6.51 at the start (the edit just removed): its build compiled the one file back (`no`, `no`, javac 1 file, `started again, empty`), then the library track ran: 86 tests, no failure, `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`, 5 min 23 s, results in `TEST-RESULTS/fast-library/`. The build stamp afterwards was again `21f2b962...`. `testCompiler`, `testOtherCompiler` and `testQuick` were not run; they use the same macro, two or three times in parallel as `testFast` does.
474:- Line 133: "Warning: `ant testCompiler`, `ant testLibrary` and `ant testOtherCompiler` also exist, but each runs `ant compileAll` first, which deletes the tree's caches." Should say: "`ant testCompiler` (compiler and othercompiler tracks), `ant testOtherCompiler`, `ant testLibrary` and `ant testQuick` (the three) run testFast's tracks of their corpus, with the same JVMs and private caches, after the build."
475:- Lines 135-141, the recipe to run one track by hand: should give `ant testLibrary` (or `testOtherCompiler`, `testCompiler`) in its place.
496:Outside the skill, three texts still say one thread for the suites or their tools: the gate prompt of `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:1839` ("The gate is pinned to one thread - env.sh:6 and, since 2026-09-19, the fastTrack and systemShard macros themselves"), `explorations/experiment/env.sh:6` (`export FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, the default for direct runs in a shell that sources it) and `explorations/coordinator/tools/count-run/count-run.sh:23`. FACTS' entry "`ant compileAll` leaves the bytecode cache holding no library jars" should name `cleanCache` as the cause (section 2) and say that the build now deletes the caches only when the implementation changes.
500:### 8.1 Tracks and shards that start from a filled cache (item 5): measured, not built
502:The measurement: right after the final cold `ant testFast` (section 6), the three compiled tracks ran again on the private caches that run had left (`tmp/warm.xml`, scratch: the `fastTrack` macro three times in parallel, no delete). The same for `ant testSystem`'s four shards. Shell without `JAVA_FLAGS`, build `767ba4a3b`.
506:| compiler track | 515 s | 274 s |
507:| library track | 344 s | 57 s |
508:| othercompiler track | 354 s | 138 s |
509:| wall of the compiled tracks | 8 min 42 s (`testFast`, with misc) | 4 min 35 s |
513:What the cold tracks spend on filling: the first test of each compiled track took 137 to 139 s (`InheritedAbstractMethodStaticParamSameName` 29.6 + 107.2 s in compiler, `IntLiteralArithRung7` 139.3 s in library, `TupleCastPass` 28.4 + 108.3 s in othercompiler); that is the library's analysis and compile, a quarter to two fifths of each track. The warm runs also skip each test's own compile, which is why they save more than that.
517:- A warm track reuses entries by Fortress's own date check. That check has a known hole on the compiled path: compiling a program never rebuilds a library component that is already in the cache, even when its source is newer (`build-cache-exploration.md`, section 2). The library and othercompiler tracks have no test that compiles the library explicitly; only the compiler track has (`CompilerBuiltinComponent.test`, `CompilerLibraryComponent.test`). So a track seeded from an earlier run, or from `default_repository/caches`, would run a library edit's tests against the old library jars, with no warning, and the gate could pass a broken library. The same hole applies to a test's own imported test components.
518:- A seed that is never wrong must therefore be keyed on the build stamp and on every Fortress source the tracks read (the library, and the test folders), as `harness-one.sh`'s cache is keyed (4.1). Such a seed is valid only when neither the implementation nor the Fortress sources changed since it was filled. The gate runs only after a change, and the record already skips a gate when no code changed (`build-cache-exploration.md`, sections 4 and 5). A worker runs a suite after its own edit. So a valid seed would exist almost only for a repeated run of one code state, for example to look for a flaky test.
519:- A seed of the library alone (the library order into a folder, copied into each track) would be valid after a test-only edit too. Making it costs the library order, about 115 s, before the tracks start; the tracks today fill in parallel, in about 137 s. So for one run it saves about 20 s of wall time, and it adds the question whether the library order's jars equal what each track compiles for itself, which nothing here shows.
540:4. **Item 5 stays unbuilt.** What it changes: the tracks and shards keep starting empty. Default: yes. Revisit if repeated suite runs on one code state become common (for example, hunting flaky tests at four threads), where reusing the whole earlier run halves both suites (8.1).

#!/bin/bash
# harness-one.sh <scratch-dir> <file.fss>... : rung C's harness-one.sh (explorations/compile-ladder/
# rung-interp-coercion/, itself rung I's shape): the testSystem harness (SystemJUTest, the class build.xml's
# testSystem shards run) over a directory holding only the named test files, with the JVM settings of
# build.xml's systemShard macro and a private cache. Run from FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh.
#
# The scratch directory is deleted when the call starts and when it ends. The private cache is the folder
# <scratch-dir>.cache beside it, kept between calls. A call starts from what that folder holds when it was
# filled under the implementation now built (ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp, which ant compileAll
# writes) and from the Fortress sources now on the source path outside the scratch directory (the .fss and
# .fsi files of Library, ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin, ProjectFortress/test_library and ProjectFortress);
# otherwise it empties the folder first. COLD_CACHE=1 empties it in any case. The folder is stamped only when
# the JVM ends normally, so a call that is killed leaves it to be emptied by the next one.
set -u
S=$(realpath -m -- "${1:?scratch dir}") ; shift
FH=${FORTRESS_HOME:?}
C=$S.cache
BUILT=$FH/ProjectFortress/build/implementation.stamp
sources_key () {
    ( cd "$FH" && { find Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin ProjectFortress/test_library -type f -name '*.fs[si]' -print0
                    find ProjectFortress -maxdepth 1 -type f -name '*.fs[si]' -print0 ; } \
        | sort -z | xargs -0 -r sha1sum | sha1sum | cut -c1-40 )
}
key () { [ -f "$BUILT" ] && echo "$(head -1 "$BUILT") sources $(sources_key)" ; }
rm -rf "$S" ; mkdir -p "$S/tests" "$S/tmp"
KEY=$(key)
if [ -z "${COLD_CACHE:-}" ] && [ -n "$KEY" ] && [ "$(cat "$C/harness.stamp" 2>/dev/null)" = "$KEY" ]; then
    CACHE=filled
else
    rm -rf "$C" ; mkdir -p "$C" ; printf '\0\0\0\0' > "$C/global.map" ; CACHE=empty
fi
rm -f "$C/harness.stamp"
for f in "$@" ; do cp "$f" "$S/tests/" ; done
CP=$("$FH/bin/fortress_classpath" 2>/dev/null | tail -1)
echo "# harness-one $(date -u +%FT%TZ); tree $(git -C "$FH" rev-parse --short HEAD); nproc=$(nproc); load $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=4; cache $CACHE"
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress" && FORTRESS_THREADS=4 FORTRESS_JUNIT_VERBOSE=1 FORTRESS_CACHES="$C" \
  java -Xmx768m -Xss32m -Djava.io.tmpdir="$S/tmp" -Dfortress.caches="$C" -Dtests="$S/tests" \
       -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.tests.unit_tests.SystemJUTest 2>&1 | grep -v '^\s*at ' | sed "s#$FH/##g"
RC=${PIPESTATUS[0]}
echo "exit=$RC"
# The cache is stamped only if the run ended normally and nothing it is keyed on changed meanwhile.
[ "$RC" = 0 ] && [ -n "$KEY" ] && [ "$(key)" = "$KEY" ] && echo "$KEY" > "$C/harness.stamp"
rm -rf "$S"
